title: What's this? — and why a book is feminine
title_target: यह क्या है? — yeh kyaa hai?
goal: Point at things and name them, ask questions with क्या, and face the first truly foreign idea in Hindi: every noun has a gender.
bekal: ask यह क्या है? and answer it
tell यह, वह, ये, and वे apart
make yes/no questions with क्या in front
guess a noun's gender from its ending
choose अच्छा or अच्छी to match the thing

dialogs.title: संवाद — The new room
dialogs.intro: Priya shows Ani her new room. The conversation seems to be just naming things, but in line eight Ani hits the first wall of Hindi — and her reaction will very likely be yours too.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: very — good — is! this — what — is?

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: This is a wardrobe. And that's a table.
lines.literal: this — wardrobe — is. and — that — table — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Wardrobe… table… these Hindi words are easy!
lines.literal: wardrobe… table… these — Hindi — words — easy — are!

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: Yes! Chair, shirt, soap — they're all in your language too.
lines.literal: yes! chair, shirt, soap — all — your(fem.) — language — in — also — are.

lines.id: And this? Is this a book?

lines.id: Yes, it's a Hindi book. It's old, but it's good.

lines.id: A boy? A book? I don't understand.

notes: **क्या has two jobs, and its position decides which.** At the **start** of a sentence it just marks a yes/no question and isn't translated: *क्या यह किताब है?* = "Is this a book?" In the **middle** it means "what": *यह क्या है?* = "What is this?" ⚠️ Put it in the wrong place and the meaning really changes. Compare lines 2 and 6 of the dialogue.

**यह and वह mean "this/that" and also "he/she/it".** Hindi has no separate words for *he*, *she*, or *it*: यह is for what's near, वह for what's far, and both are used for things and people, men and women alike. That's a big relief — you never have to choose between "he" and "she" as you do in English.

**The plurals are ये and वे, and both also serve as a respectful form for one person.** Just like आप: *वे मेरे पिता जी हैं* = "He is my father" — one person, but the plural form, out of respect. ⚠️ In conversation वे is almost always pronounced **वो** (*vo*), and ये as **ये** (*ye*). You'll hear वो far more often than वे.

**The heart of this unit: every Hindi noun is masculine (पुल्लिंग) or feminine (स्त्रीलिंग).** It has nothing to do with meaning — किताब isn't feminine because books are feminine; it's feminine because that's how it is. ⚠️ English has nothing like this, so your mother tongue can't help you guess. What you can do: **always learn a noun together with its gender**, as one unit. The glossary at the back marks every word (m) or (f) for exactly this reason.

**Adjectives ending in -आ change; all others never do.** अच्छ**ा** कमरा / अच्छ**ी** किताब, पुरान**ा** घर / पुरान**ी** किताब, बड़**ा** / बड़**ी**, छोट**ा** / छोट**ी**. But **सुंदर** (beautiful), **ठीक** (fine), **मुश्किल** (difficult), **आसान** (easy), **साफ़** (clean), and **ज़रूरी** (necessary) stay the same in front of anything. The good news: that second group is huge, so half your adjectives are trouble-free.

**Most Perso-Arabic loanwords are feminine** — a handy coincidence. किताब, मेज़, कुर्सी, कमीज़, अलमारी, दुकान, ख़बर, आदत, सेहत, इज़्ज़त, हालत, उम्र, हवा, दुनिया: all (f). ⚠️ But don't make it a law: **जवाब, सवाल, वक़्त, मतलब, मक़सद, क़ानून, फ़ायदा** are all (m). Treat it as a hint that's often right, not a rule.

**हे भगवान ("O God") is a normal, inoffensive exclamation**, but it has a Hindu flavor. Neutral equivalents everyone uses: **अरे!** (*a-re* — hey!), **अरे यार** (*a-re yaar* — oh man), **ओह हो**. Indian Muslims say **या अल्लाह** or **मा शा अल्लाह**. All of these sound far more natural than a word-for-word "oh my goodness".

grammars.title: Guessing gender: three hints and one warning
body: No rule is always right, but these three hints cover most of the nouns you'll meet at A1.

head: Hint
Examples that follow it
Examples that BREAK it
rows: कमरा, लड़का, केला, दरवाज़ा, पैसा, रास्ता
माता, दादा (m, male people), भाषा (f), दुनिया (f)
आदत, सेहत, इज़्ज़त, बारिश, मेज़, कमीज़

after: ⚠️ Look at the second row: **masculine nouns that don't end in -आ don't change at all in the plural.** घर means "house" and "houses" — only the verb (है vs. हैं) and the adjective show the difference. Think of English *sheep* or *fish*; you'll get used to it fast.

grammars.title: Pointing: यह, वह, ये, वे
after: To answer "what's this?" you don't need to repeat यह: just **किताब है** or even **किताब**. Answering in a full sentence sounds like a textbook.

sections.title: Things around you, grouped by gender

blocks.text: The cheapest way to learn genders is in groups, not one by one. Read each column aloud once a day for three days, and the groups will stick on their own.

blocks.title: Example sentences that show the difference
items: **यह कमरा बड़ा है।** — This room is big. (कमरा masculine → बड़ा)
**यह किताब बड़ी है।** — This book is big. (किताब feminine → बड़ी)
**ये कमरे बड़े हैं।** — These rooms are big. (masculine plural → बड़े)
**ये किताबें बड़ी हैं।** — These books are big. (feminine plural → still बड़ी)
⚠️ Look at the last line: **the feminine form doesn't change again in the plural.** Feminine has only one form (बड़ी for both), masculine has more (बड़ा · बड़े). Feminine is actually easier.

blocks.text: A comfort before you start to worry. Noun gender is the **most forgiven** part of Hindi. If you say *यह किताब अच्छा है*, everyone still understands and nobody will interrupt. Compare that with the retroflex sounds, which really do turn one word into another. So learn genders calmly, fix them as you go, and don't let them stop you talking.
